Addition polymerization (or chain-growth polymerization) is a process where monomers containing double or triple bonds add together to form long-chain polymers without the elimination of any small by-products (like water or $\text{HCl}$). It typically proceeds via a free-radical, cationic, or anionic mechanism in three distinct stages:

1. **Initiation:** Generation of active free radicals or ions using an initiator (e.g., benzoyl peroxide). The initiator attacks the monomer's double bond to form an active species.
   $$\text{R-R} \rightarrow 2\text{R}^•$$ 
   $$\text{R}^• + \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2-\text{CH}_2^•$$

2. **Propagation:** Rapid successive addition of large numbers of monomer molecules to the active center, extending the polymer chain.
   $$\text{R-(CH}_2-\text{CH}_2)_n-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2^• + \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{R-(CH}_2-\text{CH}_2)_{n+1}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2^•$$

3. **Termination:** Deactivation of the growing chain by combination (coupling) or disproportionation to yield the final stable polymer molecule.
